segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Hello, this is 6 Minute English from BBC Learning English. I'm Phil.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And I'm Pippa. In this episode we're discussing etiquette, the rules about what makes polite behaviour,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: and in particular the do's and don'ts about what you should and shouldn't do when eating.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: So Phil, what's the worst thing someone can do while eating, in your opinion?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: For me, it's being very noisy when you do it. I can't stand it.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Okay. I don't have too many rules about eating, but I was always told growing up that you shouldn't have your elbows on the table.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And I never really understood why, but I always remember that one.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: So we'll be hearing more about mealtime manners from some college students and an expert on British etiquette.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And as usual, we'll be learning some useful new words and phrases, all of which you can find on our website, bbclearningenglish.com.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: But first, I have a question for you, Pippa. Ideas about polite behaviour change a lot from country to country.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: So, when BBC programme The Food Chain asked listeners from around the world about eating manners in their country, what do you think was the most common complaint?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Was it a people eating with their hands b people eating noisily or c people burping at the table

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I don think it people eating with their hands because lots of people around the world do that as kind of their normal way of eating But maybe it B people eating noisily

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: I think. Like you mentioned, Phil, that's quite annoying.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Well, we'll find out the answer later

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: in the programme. The food chain also interviewed students at London's City of Westminster College

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: about family dinner times. Samuel is 19 and from Sierra Leone, and Aya is 18 and British,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: but her family are from Iraq.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Let's listen as they chat with BBC World Service's The Food Chain.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Yeah, I would say first impressions really do matter

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: because it also is really important how you portray yourself,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: how you present yourself to the person.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: What I don't want to see is any loud chewing

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: or with your mouth open, please and thank you.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: I would like to see, though, eye contact,

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: having a conversation, using your cutlery.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: sometimes and I thought this could be like picky for everyone else but having a tissue or a napkin

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: on your lap just in case you spill anything. The students think etiquette is important. Samuel says

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: it's about making a good first impression. Your first impression is the opinion you form about

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: someone when you meet them for the first time.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: For Aya eating with your mouth open is definitely rude.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: She also thinks people should use a napkin, although that could be seen as picky.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Picky here means being too strict about the rules.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: For this group of students showing respect and appreciation for the meal is very important And this idea is common across most if not all cultures throughout history

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: So imagine a scene from a TV show like Game of Thrones Two enemy forces have stopped fighting

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: made peace and now gather for a meal. The leaders clink glasses, meaning they lift up and touch

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: drinks and make a toast. They hold up a glass of alcohol and drink it to show respect.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Now keep that image in mind because we're going to hear British etiquette coach Rupert Wesson explaining why people clink glasses.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Here he is talking to Ruth Alexander, presenter of BBC World Service programme The Food Chain.

segments.speaker: Rupert Wesson
segments.text: Perhaps the simplest example is why do we clink glasses when we have a toast?

segments.speaker: Rupert Wesson
segments.text: If you clink glasses you're slopping a bit of your drink into his cup and he's slopping a bit of drink into your cup.

segments.speaker: Rupert Wesson
segments.text: and therefore by having that toast you are showing look I trust you, you trust me and that's why we do it.

segments.speaker: Ruth Alexander
segments.text: If you've poisoned my drink that's now slopped into your cup you won't drink it.

segments.speaker: Rupert Wesson
segments.text: Correct.

segments.speaker: Ruth Alexander
segments.text: Hats at the table, we're hearing from BBC World Service listeners that that is a no-no, is that right?

segments.speaker: Ruth Alexander
segments.text: It's not something I would do, in fact I would not be wearing a hat inside anyway.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: So, Phil, when we clink glasses in a toast, some of my drink might spill into your glass

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: and some of your drink might spill into mine. Historically, this mixing of drinks was a way

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: of proving the drinks were not poisoned.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Ruth also asks about wearing hats at the table and Rupert calls this a no A no is an informal phrase for something that is considered socially unacceptable

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Etiquette varies a lot over time and culture but the essential point is always to show appreciation by doing some things and avoiding others

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: And speaking of things to avoid, what was the answer to your question, Phil?

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, well, I asked you what listeners of the food chain thought was the biggest etiquette problem when people are eating.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: You said that it was people eating noisily and I can reveal that's the right answer.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: It was people eating noisily.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: OK, let's recap the vocabulary we've learnt about mealtime do's and don'ts.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: Rules about how you should and shouldn't behave.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: Your first impression of someone is the opinion you form when meeting them for the first time.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: The word picky is used to describe someone who is too strict about rules.

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: If you clink glasses, you touch two drinking glasses together as a gesture of friendship,

segments.speaker: Pippa
segments.text: probably because you're making a toast, a show of respect that involves drinking from a glass of alcohol.

segments.speaker: Phil
segments.text: And finally, a no-no is an informal word for something considered socially unacceptable.
